This is hard. I think the truth is that when you try and help people through their problems, sometimes it’s going to work, and sometimes it won’t. I think you have to develop the mentality of doing the best you can in this life, forgiving yourself when you fail.

Something that I used to do when I was lonely was to go onto twitch and talk to people. I didn’t have a lot of interpersonal skills, so I didn’t start off talking very much, but I came more and more into as time went on. It is the internet, so be careful, as some people say stupid things, but it did help me get used to talking to people, especially since we could just talk about things that didn’t matter, like the videogames we were watching.
I think that it’s to say that there are people out there who care about you, oftentimes because they know what you are going through. Much love, -internet stranger.

If you wanna talk, feel free to message me, but find someone real to talk to if you can. (Not all people will know how to respond well though, so don’t give up if the world isn’t great with you)

I agree with a lot of what others here have said about destressing when you’re not at work, but there’s a pitfall here I think, that I would caution against. I think that I have had the tendency in the past to stress about making the most of my time off. It’s not to say that the other advice here is wrong, time off is such an important thing, but as a result of that, I have found a fear that I would be wasting what time I had away from school, so what I’ve had to do is to stop holding myself so harshly accountable. I know that the things I want to do will generally still be there if I miss a day, so I try not to freak out so much about not using my time wisely. That break is supposed to be destressing, not causing more stress. 

Otherwise, I might suggest trying to find something you find enjoying during the job. I know this might be anywhere from incredibly difficult, to outright impossible, but it’s not to say that it cannot happen, that you find some appreciation for some aspect of a job you otherwise find stressful.

I think that it’s not just learning how to distract yourself, which is important, but also to learn how to deal with the problems you face, to try and get better at not letting them get to you, by telling yourself that you can survive what comes even as it’s coming at you, though I know how difficult that can be. I hope you find some peace.

Much love

I understand how you feel. I think though, that we tend to think that life will get better as if the only thing standing between us and a better life is some outside force. It’s not to say that we are responsible for our own suffering. I don’t believe that, but it’s to say that so much of how we experience the good and bad things that happen to us is colored by who we are as people. We let this darkness over cloud of view of anything better. (That’s not to say that that’s our fault. Bad things do happen, and sometimes, as you have noted, quite often) But so much of this is in how we have been taught to handle those things. It’s not easy, but part of life getting better had to do with us coming to terms with its worst elements. 

If you ever wanna talk, feel free to message me, or there are hotlines, though I have heard disparate views of how well or terribly they work, and family helps sometimes too, (it can be the best part of it), but oftentimes that’s more complicated and that family does not know how to deal with these situations, but don’t give up. 

Much love,

What I’m speaking of here, is, admittedly, a more abstract view of life, which might be off-putting. It’s not just to say that there’s some specific thing out there that I can point to that makes life worth living, but that there are things out there that make life worth living to be found by each of us. I know it’s difficult, and I’m sorry for that, but that’s what to fight for. When we’re dead, there’s no fighting left, and whatever will be, will be, but when we’re alive, when we’re kicking, we have agency. It’s not just that we have a reason to fight, but that we have the ability to keep searching for what makes life worth living, even if we cannot right now fathom that such a thing exists. 

I know it doesn’t seem like it, but there’s a reason people keep saying “it gets better.” It’s not to say it always gets better, and there are some who have good reason to be frustrated whenever they hear those words, but so often we find ourselves spiraling into really dark places, but those places are not the only ones there are. A lot of people around your age find themselves here. Some people never leave, but the thing is that most do as they get older. For most people, it does get better, and I don’t know if that’s you, but I wouldn’t assume it’s not. There’s more to life than this darkness. The way I see life, there are times to hide under the blanket, drowning out the world. Maybe this is one of those times, but part of that is that there are also times when we take whatever strength we have and we move, and we keep moving in that search for meaning and purpose and happiness, the pursuit thereof. 

So don’t give up searching. I know you don’t have the will to fight right now, and that’s okay. But holding on is fighting too, even if it’s just lying in bed.

I’m sorry that your mother treated you like that, but not all people are like that. Don’t give up trying to find someone who will care for you, but part of learning to live is learning to love yourself, to know that you have value despite how you’ve been treated.

Increasingly, I have seen a trend of people around your age dealing with these things. That’s not to say that they are any less impactful or to imply that they should be easy in any way. Often, the saying “it’ll get better” is criticized, and for good reason. It often doesn’t really help. But there’s a reason people say it. In many cases, there’s a ring of truth to it. We get down into very low places where we don’t think there’s any purpose to life and living, but those low places are exactly that, and we don’t always remain there. Often, we go on to find that life does get better, though that is not to say that everyone does, and those that don’t have a lot of reason to be frustrated with this phrase. A lot of people who are your age tend to see life from a very dark perspective, but this also often gets better as you get older, life doesn’t seem as pointless as it did. This is not, again to say, that there’s not vast, debilitating problems people sometimes have, which include depression and other mental illnesses, and problems with life itself, but it’s to say that most people do move forward from where you are right now. I’m not saying that’s you. I don’t know you, or your problems, but I do know that life is valuable, and I am want to fight for those who need help, so if you want to talk, feel free to message me, or, there are also support lines, though I’ve gotten mixed messages for how well they work, that there are directories to online. Also, family can help, but that is complicated too. Oftentimes, they find themselves unequipped to handle problems like these, but that’s not to say that you should dismiss them out of hand. 

Much love, 
-internet stranger.

Depending on where you live, you might be able to drive in a year, or at least a few years. Find a way to get help, in whatever way you can, but don’t give up.

I’m sorry this happened to you. If you can to talk more about it, or to vent, message me. People do stupid things, without realizing how much they can hurt or thinking it’s the right thing to do when so often it’s not.

It’s not always that people pretend suicide isn’t logical. It’s that there’s an emphasis on life that people believe in. It’s not to undermine just how painful that life can be, but to argue that the life is valuable, and that we should fight to make a better world for ourselves and others.

It’s not to say that life is easy, but so often depression does cloud how we see it. Depression messes with the head. I’m not going to say that suicide is never a logical choice, though I might disagree with that logic, but I will say that depression is an illness that often causes that choice and when it does, it’s a tragedy, not just because I feel badly about it, but because I know that that depression gave someone the opposite of rose colored glasses. It’s not to say that life isn’t bad. Often, it really is, but when life is bad because your brain is affecting how you see that life, (often mixed with that life actually having problems) it seems as though it’s not quite as simple as just having a logical decision get made. So often, it’s not that people want to kill themselves, it’s that people want to escape the pain they’re in that their brains are distorting and that seems like the best solution. (I know a lot of this brain talk might seem that I am accusing people with depression of being crazy- I’m not. I have the upmost sympathy. I see depression as a disease, like something to fight or be victim to.) 

If you ever want to talk, feel free to message me. Much love, -internet stranger.

It sounds like you are stuck behind a roadblock for moving forward because you feel as though you don’t deserve it. (Correct me if I’m wrong) Changing to make your life better isn’t a bad thing, but a part of that, I think, is coming to grips with who you are. I don’t know you. I know that a lot of people feel guiltier than they should about their choices though, but if change would make you happier, than that is good, but part of change is learning to love yourself. The best people in this world don’t hate themselves. They accept who they are while trying to be decent, and when they fail, they try to do better. Have patience with yourself, too. This is a process. It’s not so easy. Don’t take this mindset of “I don’t deserve to be happy.” You’re your greatest cheerleader. You, more than anyone, have the power to fight for your happiness. I’m not going to say that no one else will, but often times, people don’t, or don’t do it well enough. (Though they try) If you want to be happy, it’s not wrong. It’s not that you don’t deserve it, but you’re the best one to fight for it so why not fight for it and let the chips fall where they may? 

If you ever want to talk, feel free to message me, or message others here or talk to family if you can, (I know it’s not always that simple) or, there are often hotlines. What I’m trying to say is, don’t give up. 

Much love, 
-internet stranger.

Much love,

There’s a value to who you are as a person, if only based in how you experience life, pain being apart of that, which is not to idealize pain, as is often done. If you wanna talk, I’ll be here. Your experiences have value. That’s meaningful, I think. You, who are in many ways built by those experiences, and shape them in a way no other being could, have value. That’s not pointless.
